subject: History of Pakistan & India
title: 3. Constitutional and Political Reforms under the British (1858–1947)

segments.text: This topic is the constitutional spine connecting the aftermath of 1857 (Topic 2) to the Pakistan Movement (Topic 5) and to Pakistan’s own post-1947 constitution-making (Topic 6). Every later Pakistani and Indian constitutional debate — about federalism, about minority representation, about the balance between central and provincial power — has direct roots in the reforms studied here. The examiner’s real question across this topic is never simply “what did each reform grant?” but always the paired question: “what did the British still keep, and why did Indian political opinion consider that insufficient?”

blocks.text: Background: The Logic of Gradual, Controlled Reform

segments.text: After 1858, British policy toward Indian political participation followed a consistent underlying logic: expand consultative and, later, representative institutions gradually, in response to political pressure and changing strategic calculations (including the World Wars), while retaining ultimate control over defence, foreign affairs, and — until 1947 — the power to override or suspend Indian self-government where London judged it necessary. Every reform discussed below should be read against this pattern of controlled concession rather than a steady, linear march toward full self-government.
The
Indian Councils Act of 1861

was the first post-1857 constitutional measure. It restored and expanded the Governor-General’s legislative council by adding non-official members — for the first time including a small number of Indians — who could discuss and comment on legislation, but who had no power to vote on the budget, ask questions, or exercise any real check on executive decisions. The
Indian Councils Act of 1892

widened these councils further, allowing indirect election of some non-official members (through local bodies and associations rather than a general franchise) and permitting limited discussion of the budget and the right to ask questions — a real but still very narrow expansion of participation. Executive power in both cases remained firmly with the British-appointed Governor-General and Governors.

blocks.text: The Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909: Wider Councils, Separate Electorates

segments.text: The Indian Councils Act 1909, commonly called the Morley-Minto reforms after the Secretary of State (John Morley) and Viceroy (Lord Minto) who negotiated them, substantially enlarged legislative councils at both the central and provincial level and expanded their power to discuss budgets and move resolutions, though executive responsibility to the legislature was still not established — councils could advise and criticise, but the executive did not depend on their confidence.
The reform’s most consequential and most debated feature was the introduction of
separate electorates for Muslims

: Muslim voters would elect Muslim representatives to a fixed number of reserved seats, rather than voting in general constituencies alongside Hindu and other voters. This decision followed the Simla Deputation of 1906 (in which a delegation of Muslim leaders petitioned Viceroy Minto for separate representation, discussed in depth in Topic 4) and is one of the single most important constitutional developments in the entire syllabus, because it formally linked constitutional design to communal identity for the first time and set a precedent — separate electorates, and later weightage and reserved seats — that shaped every subsequent constitutional negotiation through to partition itself. Nationalist Congress opinion generally opposed separate electorates as an instrument of the colonial strategy sometimes summarised as “divide and rule,” while a significant body of Muslim political opinion regarded them as a necessary safeguard against permanent minority status in an eventual system of majority rule. Both positions need to be understood, not merely stated, to answer questions on this reform well.

blocks.text: The Path to 1919: Repression Alongside Reform

segments.text: The First World War (1914–1918) changed the political calculation on both sides. India contributed heavily to the British war effort in manpower and resources, and Indian political leaders expected meaningful constitutional reward in return. In August 1917, Secretary of State Edwin Montagu announced in the British Parliament that the goal of British policy was the “gradual development of self-governing institutions” leading toward “responsible government” in India — the first explicit British statement of self-government as an eventual goal, though without a timetable.
At almost the same moment, however, the colonial state moved toward greater repression: the
Rowlatt Act of 1919
extended emergency wartime powers of detention without trial into peacetime, provoking widespread protest. Protests against the Rowlatt Act in Amritsar led to the
Jallianwala Bagh massacre

of April 1919, in which troops under General Reginald Dyer fired without warning on an unarmed crowd gathered in an enclosed garden, killing several hundred people (estimates vary; British official figures and Indian estimates differ substantially, and the exact toll remains a matter of historical dispute, though the scale of the atrocity itself is not in question). This episode radicalised a generation of Indian political opinion and is essential context for understanding why the reforms announced the same year were widely regarded as inadequate — reform and repression arrived almost simultaneously, and the repression made the limits of the reform far harder to accept.

blocks.text: The Government of India Act 1919: Dyarchy

segments.text: The Government of India Act 1919 introduced the system of
dyarchy

(“dual government”) at the provincial level: provincial subjects were divided into “transferred” subjects (such as education, health and local self-government), administered by Indian ministers responsible to the enlarged provincial legislature, and “reserved” subjects (such as police, justice and revenue), which remained under the direct control of the Governor and his executive council, not answerable to the legislature. This was a genuine, if partial, experiment in representative provincial government — the first time elected Indian ministers held real executive authority over some areas of provincial policy — but the retention of the most sensitive functions (police, revenue, law and order) under unaccountable executive control meant that “self-government” remained heavily qualified. At the centre, the Act created a bicameral legislature (a Legislative Assembly and a Council of State) with expanded Indian membership, but the central government remained fully answerable to the Viceroy and, through him, to London rather than to the Indian legislature.

blocks.text: The Government of India Act 1935: Provincial Autonomy and the Unrealised Federation

segments.text: The Government of India Act 1935 was the most extensive constitutional framework produced before partition, and it operated in two quite different registers:

items.text: Provincial autonomy

, which actually came into force, abolished dyarchy and gave provincial legislatures and Indian ministers real, accountable control over the entire range of provincial subjects (subject to certain “special responsibilities” retained by Governors, such as the ability to intervene to protect minority rights or maintain law and order in genuine emergencies, but these were meant to be reserve powers rather than routine controls). This allowed the 1937 provincial elections and the resulting Congress ministries, which are central to Topic 5.
An all-India federation
, which was proposed but
never came into operation

, would have combined British India’s provinces with the princely states in a federal structure with a bicameral central legislature. It failed chiefly because a sufficient number of princely states never acceded to the scheme (many rulers feared loss of autonomy and revenue), and the outbreak of the Second World War in 1939 further postponed any implementation. Students frequently confuse the (implemented) provincial-autonomy provisions with the (never-implemented) federal provisions of the same Act — keeping these two halves of the Act clearly separate is one of the highest-value distinctions in this entire topic.

segments.text: The 1935 Act also expanded the franchise considerably (to roughly one-sixth of the adult population, still far short of universal suffrage) and extended separate electorates to additional categories beyond Muslims, including a separate electorate scheme for the “depressed classes” (the subject of the Communal Award and Poona Pact, discussed below).

blocks.text: The Indian National Congress: From Petition to Mass Movement

segments.text: The
Indian National Congress
, founded in 1885 largely at the initiative of the retired British civil servant Allan Octavian Hume together with prominent Indian professionals, began as a
moderate

organisation whose early leaders (such as Dadabhai Naoroji, discussed in Topic 2’s “drain of wealth” argument, and Gopal Krishna Gokhale) petitioned for greater Indian representation in the civil service and legislative councils, and pursued reform through constitutional argument and loyal petition rather than mass mobilisation.
By the early twentieth century, a more assertive
“Extremist”

faction emerged, associated with leaders such as Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal and Lala Lajpat Rai (together often called “Lal-Bal-Pal”), who argued for more direct methods including boycott of British goods and swadeshi (self-reliant, indigenous economic activity) — a strategy that gained enormous force in reaction to the 1905 Partition of Bengal (covered in Topic 4). Tensions between Moderates and Extremists led to a formal split within Congress in 1907, later partially healed.
Annie Besant and Tilak separately launched
Home Rule Leagues

during the First World War, demanding self-government within the British Empire along the lines of Ireland or the self-governing dominions — an important bridge between earlier petition-based politics and the mass politics that followed.
Mahatma Gandhi’s

return to India from South Africa in 1915, and his emergence as the dominant Congress leader from around 1919–1920, marked a decisive shift toward genuinely mass-based, nonviolent political mobilisation: the
Non-Cooperation Movement
(1920–1922, temporarily allied with the Khilafat Movement discussed in Topic 4, and called off by Gandhi after the violent Chauri Chaura incident in 1922), the
Civil Disobedience Movement
(1930–1934, including the famous Salt March of 1930), and the
Quit India Movement

(1942, launched during the Second World War, met with immediate mass arrests of Congress leadership and severe repression). Each of these movements pressured the colonial government toward further constitutional concession, even where the immediate movement itself was suppressed — a pattern worth stating explicitly, since it explains the causal link between mass politics and constitutional reform that a purely legalistic account of the Acts alone would miss.

blocks.text: The Communal Award and the Poona Pact (1932)

segments.text: At the Second Round Table Conference (1931, discussed further in Topic 5), the failure of Indian delegates to agree on a scheme of minority representation led British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald to announce the
Communal Award

in 1932, extending separate electorates not only to Muslims but also to Sikhs, Christians, Anglo-Indians, and, most controversially, the “depressed classes” (those subject to untouchability under the caste system, represented in the negotiations by B. R. Ambedkar). Gandhi, who opposed separating the depressed classes from the general Hindu electorate on the grounds that this would permanently fragment Hindu political unity, undertook a fast in protest; the resulting negotiation between Gandhi and Ambedkar produced the
Poona Pact

(1932), which replaced separate electorates for the depressed classes with a system of reserved seats within general electorates — depressed-class candidates would be elected, but by the whole general electorate rather than by depressed-class voters alone. This episode is a useful, self-contained case study of how communal representation disputes could be genuinely negotiated and resolved, in contrast to the Muslim-Congress disagreement over separate electorates, which was never similarly resolved before partition.

items.text: Dyarchy:
The division of provincial government (under the 1919 Act) into “transferred” subjects under accountable Indian ministers and “reserved” subjects under the unaccountable Governor’s executive.
Provincial autonomy:
The 1935 Act’s grant of full, accountable ministerial control over all provincial subjects, replacing dyarchy.
Separate electorate:
A system in which members of a specified community vote only for candidates of their own community in reserved constituencies.
Communal Award:
The 1932 British decision extending separate or reserved representation to several minority communities, including the depressed classes.
Poona Pact:
The 1932 Gandhi–Ambedkar agreement replacing separate depressed-class electorates with reserved seats within general electorates.

blocks.text: Historiographical Debates: Why Did Reform Happen?

segments.text: Historians disagree, in revealing ways, about what actually drove this sequence of reforms:

items.text: The
“Cambridge School”

of historians (associated especially with Anil Seal, John Gallagher and Gordon Johnson) emphasised the internal factional and patronage politics of Indian elites competing for access to colonial institutions, arguing that constitutional concessions were substantially shaped by the colonial state’s own strategic calculations about which Indian groups to co-opt as “collaborators,” rather than being simple, direct responses to nationalist pressure from below.
Nationalist historiography

, by contrast, generally presents each reform primarily as a concession won through sustained political struggle and mass mobilisation — Congress agitation, the Home Rule movement, Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience — reading the sequence of Acts as a story of pressure from below gradually forcing British retreat.
Subaltern Studies historians

(from the 1980s onward) criticised both of the above frameworks for focusing almost exclusively on educated elites — whether colonial administrators or Congress leadership — and argued that the political consciousness and agency of peasants, workers and other subordinated groups deserves independent study rather than being read only through elite politics or elite-negotiated constitutional reform.

segments.text: A strong exam answer does not need to adjudicate definitively among these schools, but recognising that “why did Britain grant this reform?” has more than one serious scholarly answer — elite co-optation, nationalist pressure, or a combination shaped by wartime and economic pressures specific to each moment — will distinguish a strong answer from a purely descriptive one.
Preparation Checklist

items.text: Build a single chronological table: year, Act/reform, central structure, provincial structure, franchise/representation, and long-term significance. This is far more useful for revision than prose paragraphs learned separately for each Act.
Prepare Congress’s internal evolution (Moderates → Extremists → Home Rule → Gandhian mass politics) as its own labelled sub-timeline, since examiners frequently ask about this trajectory on its own.
Prepare the Communal Award and Poona Pact as a self-contained case study of a communal representation dispute that was resolved, useful for contrast with disputes that were not.

Keep an evidence bank: Indian Councils Act 1861 and 1892, Morley-Minto 1909, Montagu’s 1917 Declaration, Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh 1919, Government of India Act 1919, Government of India Act 1935, Communal Award and Poona Pact 1932.

Practice one analytical outline answering: “Each constitutional reform between 1861 and 1935 both granted new participation and preserved British control. Explain this pattern using at least three reforms.”

segments.text: Common Confusions to Avoid

items.text: Do not memorise Acts only by year; compare representation, executive responsibility, provincial powers and political reaction for each one.
Dyarchy (1919 Act) applies to the provincial level only; do not confuse it with the fuller provincial autonomy introduced later by the 1935 Act, which replaced dyarchy entirely.
Do not confuse the 1935 Act’s provincial-autonomy provisions (implemented, leading to the 1937 elections) with its all-India federation provisions (proposed, never implemented).

Do not equate a larger legislature with full democracy; franchise remained limited throughout this period, and Governors and the Viceroy retained significant reserve powers even under provincial autonomy.

segments.text: Easy Revision Points

items.text: The Indian Councils Acts of 1861 and 1892 gradually widened legislative councils but did not create responsible government.
The Indian Councils Act 1909 (Morley-Minto reforms) introduced separate electorates for Muslims.
The Government of India Act 1919 introduced dyarchy in the provinces and expanded legislatures, against the backdrop of the Rowlatt Act and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre the same year.
The Government of India Act 1935 provided provincial autonomy (implemented) and proposed an all-India federation (never implemented).
The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885 and evolved from Moderate petitioning through Extremist agitation and the Home Rule movement to Gandhian mass politics from around 1920 onward.
The Communal Award (1932) and the resulting Poona Pact between Gandhi and Ambedkar resolved the specific dispute over depressed-class representation.
Every constitutional reform in this period should be read on two levels at once: what it granted, and what the British still retained — that paired question is the examiner’s real interest.

The Morley-Minto reforms’ introduction of separate electorates for Muslims in 1909 is the single most consequential constitutional decision in this topic, since it set a precedent for communal representation that shaped every subsequent negotiation through to partition.

The 1919 and 1935 Acts must be kept structurally distinct — dyarchy versus full provincial autonomy — and the 1935 Act’s two halves (implemented provincial autonomy, unimplemented federation) must also be kept distinct from each other.

The Indian National Congress’s internal evolution, from Moderate petitioning to Extremist agitation to Gandhian mass mobilisation, is itself an important sub-narrative, and mass movements (Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, Quit India) should be understood as a causal pressure behind constitutional change, not a separate story.

Historians genuinely disagree about what drove this reform sequence — elite co-optation, nationalist pressure, or a mix shaped by wartime pressures — and a strong answer shows awareness of this debate rather than assuming reform was simply Britain’s gradual, voluntary concession of self-government.
